cards.explanation: The answer is that God would hurry to help him, friends. David opens with “Make haste, O God, to deliver me! Hurry, O LORD, to help me!” He says what he needs, twice, and I respect a man who gets to the point.

The answer is True, friends. David prays, “May those who seek my life be ashamed and confounded…” These are people who are after his life, and he asks that they be ashamed. He brings it to God as a prayer.

The answer is that they rejoice and be glad in God, friends. David prays, “May all who seek You rejoice and be glad in You…” He's just been talking about people who want him gone, and now he turns to the people who want God. His wish for them is joy.
The answer is God, friends. David says to God, “You are my help and my deliverer…” He calls himself poor and needy, and then he says who his help is. He doesn't point to himself.
The answer is False, bakers. David's last words in Psalm 70 are “O LORD, do not delay.” He started the psalm asking God to hurry and he finishes the same way. The prayer is bookended by hurry.
The answer is God's justice, friends. The writer prays, “In Your justice, rescue and deliver me…” He's leaning on who God is, not on anything about himself. That's a solid place to stand.

The answer is his rock and his fortress, friends. He says to God, “…for You are my rock and my fortress.” Both are things you run to when trouble comes. Rock, fortress, refuge: he's piling up places to be safe.

The answer is birth, bakers. The writer says, “I have leaned on You since birth…” He's looking back over his whole life and he can't find a time he wasn't leaning on God. That's a long stretch of leaning.
The answer is praise, friends. The writer says, “My mouth is filled with Your praise and with Your splendor all day long.” All day long, bakers. That's a mouth with a full schedule and no complaints.
The answer is that God has forsaken him, friends. His enemies say, “God has forsaken him…” Notice who is saying it. It's the enemies talking, and the writer is the one praying for God to stay near.

The answer is True, friends. His enemies say no one will rescue him, and he turns to God and prays, “Be not far from me, O God.” He answers their talk with a prayer. That's the right place to take it.
The answer is False, friends. With accusers around, he says, “But I will always hope and will praise You more and more.” He isn't going quiet and waiting it out. His praise is turning up, not down.

The answer is that he can't know their full measure, friends. He says he'll declare God's righteousness and salvation all day long, “…though I cannot know their full measure.” It's like trying to find the bottom of a bottomless cookie jar. You keep reaching in, and you never hit the end.

The answer is False, bakers. The writer says, “I will come in the strength of the Lord GOD…” So the strength is God's, not his own. Strong words from a man who earlier prayed about his strength failing.

The answer is until he tells the next generation of God's power, friends. He prays, “…do not forsake me, O God, until I proclaim Your power to the next generation…” Even old and gray, he has a job left to do. He wants to pass it on.
The answer is “Who is like You,” friends. After talking about the great things God has done, he asks, “Who, O God, is like You?” (Psalm 71:19) I think that's the sound of a man amazed.
The answer is revive, friends. The writer says, “…You will revive me once again.” He's been honest about the troubles, and he still says it. That's a hope with some weight on it.
The answer is True, bakers. The writer says, “You will increase my honor and comfort me once again.” After the troubles, he's looking ahead to honor and comfort. That's a good thing to hold on to.

The answer is His faithfulness, friends. The writer says, “So I will praise You with the harp for Your faithfulness, O my God…” He brings the harp and the lyre, and he brings the reason too. It's God's faithfulness.

The answer is his soul, which God redeemed, friends. The writer says, “When I sing praise to You my lips will shout for joy, along with my soul, which You have redeemed.” His lips and his soul are shouting together. The whole man is in the song.
